categories.name: Seasons
categories.description: The valley through the twenty-four small seasons: what flowers, what falls, what the river is doing, and what it means for the bath and the table.

tags.name: Autumn
tags.description: Maples from the pass downwards, persimmons under the eaves, mushrooms and new rice: notes from September to November.

posts.title: Persimmons on the eaves
posts.excerpt: Three hundred astringent persimmons, peeled by hand and hung under the eaves to sweeten until the first snow.
posts.content:
Every October the back porch fills with persimmons. They come from the two old trees behind the east wing and from neighbours who have more than they can eat: small, hard, astringent fruit that nobody would bite into fresh. Peeled by hand and hung on strings under the eaves, they turn sweet and soft in about five weeks.

This year we counted three hundred and twelve. Kenta peels; Mio ties; the guests in Kaede usually end up helping, because the strings hang right outside their window.

From the eaves to the tray

The first fresh persimmons go straight into the hassun of the cold-dew dinner, sliced thin with chestnut and ginkgo. The dried ones are ready by the start of winter, when Tomoe serves them with a little aged cheese from a dairy over the pass.

Nothing in the valley is in a hurry, least of all a persimmon.

Mio Okuno

If you stay with us before the end of November, ask for a string to take home. They travel well, wrapped in paper, and keep until spring.

posts.title: The river bath reopens
posts.excerpt: After three weeks of resetting stones and clearing the summer silt, Kawara-yu is open again, a little deeper than before.
posts.content:
Every few years the summer storms move the riverbed enough that the stones around the open-air bath shift. This year three of them had settled, and the pool had grown shallow at the river end.

We closed the bath for three weeks, lifted eleven stones, cleared the silt and set them again by hand, the way Kenta's grandfather first laid them in 1994. The bath is now about ten centimetres deeper, enough to sit with the water at your shoulders.

The spring itself never stopped running; for three weeks it simply went straight back to the river.

posts.title: A morning walk to the pass
posts.excerpt: Forty minutes up through the cedars, or all morning if you let it. Our favourite walk, with a map and a rice ball.
posts.content:
The trail starts behind the inn, at the stone lantern with the moss on its roof, and climbs through the cedars to the pass above the valley. It takes forty minutes at a walking pace and most of a morning at ours.

We pack a rice ball, a pickled plum and a flask of roasted tea for anyone who asks at breakfast. Mio's map marks the three benches, the spring where the water is cold enough to hurt, and the lookout where, on clear autumn mornings, you can see the mist lying in the valley like milk in a bowl.

Good shoes, please. And a bath when you come back down.

posts.title: Why we light the lanterns by hand
posts.excerpt: Seven stone lanterns, one box of matches, about twelve minutes every evening. It could be a switch. It will not be.
posts.content:
There are seven stone lanterns between the gate and the front door. Each has a candle in a glass, and each evening someone walks the path with a box of matches. In summer that happens at seven; by late October, at five.

We are often asked why we do not wire them. The honest answer is that the walk is the point: twelve minutes in the garden at dusk, checking that nothing has fallen on the path, listening to what the river is doing.

posts.title: Rain on the veranda
posts.excerpt: The rainy season is the moss garden's best month. We open every screen and let the house sound like a gutter.
posts.content:
Most guests avoid the rainy season, which is a shame for them and a quiet month for us. The moss garden is never greener; the river runs loud; the bath in a warm rain is one of the stranger pleasures of the year.

We open every screen on the corridor side and put a few cushions on the veranda. With a cup of tea and nowhere to go, an afternoon disappears.

posts.title: Breakfast from the valley
posts.excerpt: Eleven small dishes, nine of them from within a day's walk. A guided tour of the morning tray.
posts.content:
Breakfast is the meal guests photograph least and remember most. Here is what is on the tray, and where it comes from.

The fish is river trout or char, salted the night before and grilled over charcoal. The tofu is from the village, made at four in the morning by a man who has done so for forty years. The rice is from the terraces below the station; the miso is our own, two summers old; the pickles were started in 1962 and have been fed ever since.

posts.title: New robes, dyed two valleys over
posts.excerpt: Our cotton robes are now dyed with indigo by a small workshop in the next valley but one. They fade beautifully.
posts.content:
This spring we replaced the guest robes for the first time in nine years. The new ones are plain-woven cotton, dyed with indigo by a three-person workshop two valleys to the west, with a small cross pattern resisted into the cloth.

Each set is a robe, a moss-green jacket for the corridors in cold months and a persimmon sash. They will fade with every wash, which is the idea.

posts.title: Winter dates are open
posts.excerpt: December to February, snow on the roofs and yuzu in the bath. Enquiries for winter stays are open from today.
posts.content:
Winter is the season our regular guests book first, so we open the dates early. From December the valley is usually white; the road is cleared every morning and our car meets every afternoon train.

The winter dinner moves to the hearth room, around a hot pot. On the solstice we float yuzu in the cypress bath. On clear nights the river bath, with snow falling into it, is the best seat in the valley.
